newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia grains gain little in freight fall.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia grains gain little in freight fall.

text.p: A world-wide slump in shipping freight rates is expected to remain for months but payoffs for Australia's bulk grains export sector are likely to be confined to the very short-term, grains and shipping sources said.

With Australia headed for wheat exports of more than 12 million tonnes in 1996/97, a decline in freight rates to A$23 a tonne from A$27 at end-1995 on a typical east coast Australian shipment to the Middle East apparently offers the potential of tens of millions of dollars in annual freight savings.
But the potential saving does not translate in the real world, said David Stott, senior chartering officer for the Australian Wheat Board (AWB).
"I think the benefit is very limited. The penalties outweigh the benefits," he said.
The only time Australia would benefit would be in a falling market when forward sales were held. But very few of Australia's customers bought more than a month or two ahead, he said.
Australia's dilemma is compounded by the fact that only 15 to 25 percent of its grain exports are on a cost and freight basis.
Most of Australia's big wheat buyers -- Indonesia, Japan, China, Iran -- have large national flag fleets and all buy on a free on board (fob) basis, Stott pointed out.
"What they pay for their own ships to carry the grain, (we) don't know," he said.
Stott doubts that Australia's own looming bumper 1996/97 wheat harvest will be enough to cause a turnaround in the depressed freight market.
"It'll make a slight difference. Anything that uses the surplus of ships will put some upward pressure on rates," he said.
Australian new crop wheat shipments will start in October from Queensland and northern Western Australia, with shipments from elsewhere following in successive months.
But Stott sees the AWB's competition on world markets as a much more important force in the economics of wheat sales than shipping rates.
"So long as everybody's paying similar rates, it doesn't really matter if freight rates are high or low," he said.
"If prevailing freight costs are high, they are high for everyody. Nobody really benefits," he said.
And low freight rates were bad for everyone concerned because less was spent on upgrading ships.
A shipping broker who deals in grains, who asked that he not be named, expects general freight rates to remain steady in coming months.
"I can't see returns on vessels going down much further. I think the market is generally going to remain stagnant for the next four to six months," he said.
Like the AWB's Stott, the broker sees an oversupply of shipping tonnage world-wide as the primary cause of the freight rate decline, with relative lack of grain cargoes a secondary cause.
A depressed scrap market was a barrier to over-age tonnage being removed from the shipping market. New tonnage coming out of the yards outweighed what was not disappearing, he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
